content: Severe malaria is a critical medical emergency, and delays in initiating treatment can result in death. Most patients with severe malaria require parenteral treatment. In primary healthcare settings where intravenous therapy is unavailable, intramuscular quinine, artesunate, or artemether are often used before transferring patients to a hospital. However, in rural areas with limited healthcare access, even intramuscular injections may not be feasible. In such cases, rectal artesunate administered before hospital transfer by minimally trained volunteers may serve as a practical alternative. The objective of this study was to assess the impact of pre-referral rectal artesunate on mortality and morbidity in individuals with severe malaria. To achieve this, researchers conducted a systematic search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to May 21, 2014. They also reviewed the WHO clinical trial registry platform and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT) for ongoing studies. The inclusion criteria focused on individual or cluster-randomized controlled trials comparing rectal artesunate with placebo or injectable antimalarials in children and adults with severe malaria. Two independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of potential studies and extracted data from the included trials. Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Subgroup analyses were performed based on age, trial region, and participant inclusion in the trial analysis. The quality of evidence for key outcomes was assessed using the GRADE approach. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This was a placebo-controlled study involving 17,826 participants, including children and adults from rural villages in Ghana, Tanzania (Africa), and Bangladesh (Asia). Volunteers with no prior medical training were educated to identify symptoms of severe malaria, administer rectal artesunate, and refer patients to hospitals. These volunteers were supervised throughout the trial. In the African sites, only children aged 6 to 72 months were enrolled, while in Bangladesh, older children and adults were also included. In young children aged 6 to 72 months, rectal artesunate was associated with a reduction in mortality compared to placebo (RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.93; one trial; 8,050 participants; moderate-quality evidence). However, in older children and adults, mortality was higher in those who received rectal artesunate compared to placebo (RR 2.21; 95% CI 1.18 to 4.15; one trial; 4,018 participants; low-quality evidence). In Africa, only 56% of participants reached a secondary healthcare facility within six hours, whereas over 90% did so in Asia. There were no significant differences between the intervention and control groups in the proportion of participants reaching a healthcare facility within six hours (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.01; 12,068 participants), the proportion with parasitemia (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.02; 17,826 participants), or the proportion presenting with coma or convulsions upon arrival (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.14; 12,068 participants). No trials were identified that directly compared rectal artesunate with intramuscular artesunate. The authors concluded that in rural areas where injectable antimalarials are unavailable, pre-referral rectal artesunate likely reduces mortality in severely ill young children compared to referral without treatment. However, the unexpected finding of potentially higher mortality in older children and adults necessitates careful consideration when developing national or local policies regarding the use of pre-referral rectal artesunate.
